report.source_text: MRI of the brain showed hyperintense lesions in the brainstem and left caudate nucleus. These lesions were hyperintense in diffusion-weighted and apparent diffusion coefficient images. Gadolinium enhancement was absent, and MR spectroscopy showed an elevation of the choline peak and preserved N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) peak, suggesting neuroinflammation (figure 1).

report.source_text: According to the acute onset of a brainstem lesion, MRI findings and HLA-B51 positivity, we started oral corticosteroid and colchicine therapy after intravenous methylprednisolone administration (1000 mg/day for 3 days) on suspicion of neuro-Behçet’s disease.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A man in his 70s with a 40-year history of uveitis and retinitis pigmentosa (diagnosed in his 30s) and HLA-B51 homozygous allele presented with a 3-day history of acute neurological symptoms including gait disturbance, left hemiparaesthesia, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Brain MRI revealed hyperintense lesions in the brainstem and left caudate nucleus with features of neuroinflammation (elevated choline peak, preserved NAA peak on MR spectroscopy, hyperintense on DWI/ADC, no gadolinium enhancement). CSF analysis was normal without elevated IL-6, oligoclonal bands, or cytopathology abnormalities. Physical examination showed mild fever (37.2°C) but no mucocutaneous ulcers, skin rash, or pathergy response. The patient met criteria for probable neuro-Behçet's disease according to International consensus recommendation criteria based on the combination of prior ocular involvement and acute CNS manifestations with characteristic neuroinflammatory MRI findings. Treatment was initiated with intravenous methylprednisolone (1000 mg/day for 3 days) followed by oral corticosteroids and colchicine. Symptoms gradually ameliorated over 2 months, with follow-up MRI showing reduction of brain lesions. The patient was discharged with minor sequelae of mild left hemiparesis and gait disturbance.
